names.name: Where the marks go
names.said: Counted across every tradition on the site

text.what: Each tradition here records which zones of the body it marks. Counted together, the zones sort into two kinds.
text.story:
**Zones that can be covered** — thighs, back, chest, waist-to-knee — belong to traditions where the tattoo is a garment and the wearer chooses when it is seen. **Zones that cannot** — face, chin, hands, fingers — belong to traditions where the mark is an identification, and where a state that wanted the practice stopped could enforce the ban by looking at people.

*Inference —* the second group is where the bans land. Chin faces, Atayal faces, Okinawan hands, Ainu mouths, Māori chins. The leg traditions were not banned; they faded. **A mark you cannot hide is easy to police, and a mark under a longyi is not worth the trouble.**
text.notes: Counted from the `placement` field on every tradition record; the chart prints how many records carried the field.

when.label: Banned by the Union Revolutionary Council

text.what: Burma's socialist government banned Chin facial tattooing in the 1960s; missionaries had been discouraging it for decades already.
text.story:
The practice ended inside a generation. The women who carry it were tattooed as teenagers before the ban and are now in their seventies and eighties, and they are photographed constantly.

*Inference —* a ban works fastest on a mark that is made once, in youth, by a specialist. Stop the specialists for twenty years and there is nobody left who has done it.

names.name: The tattoo is clothing
names.said: Three languages, three centuries, three continents, one metaphor

text.what: Sources in Burmese, Northern Thai, Spanish and Samoan — and a Cordilleran rule recorded in English — reach for the same comparison: the tattoo is not on the body, it is what the body wears.
text.story:
Shway Yoe, Burma, 1882, on the finished *htoe kwin*: the effect is "not so much of a marking of the cuticle as of **a skin-tight pair of caleçons**, fitting better than the best glove ever made."

A Lanna volume, northern Thailand, describing the same region's work from its own side: men tattooed their bodies **จนดูเหมือนนุ่งกางเกงสีดำ** — "until it looked as if they wore black trousers" — and a man with no marks should put on a woman's skirt instead.

A Spanish account of the Visayans: a naked tattooed man "appears to be **dressed in a kind of handsome armor** engraved with very fine work… their dress at home and in their barrio is their tattoos and a *bahag*."

The Cordillerans: having no tattoos was **equated to being naked**. The Samoans: an untattooed man is **telefua** or **telenoa** — naked, in the ordinary word, not as a figure of speech.

*Inference —* this is the one comparison that survives translation everywhere on this map, and it is doing work. A garment is the thing that makes a person presentable in public; it is put on at a particular age; its absence is shameful rather than merely unusual; and it is the first thing another person reads. Every one of those is also true of the marks. **Where a tradition covers a whole zone of the body, its own sources describe that zone as dressed.**
text.notes: The count of traditions on this site whose sources use the clothing comparison is computed at build time and printed on the page rather than asserted here.

text_th.what: แหล่งข้อมูลภาษาพม่า ภาษาเหนือ สเปน และซามัว รวมถึงกติกาของชาวคอร์ดิลเยราที่บันทึกไว้เป็นภาษาอังกฤษ เลือกคำเปรียบเดียวกัน รอยสักไม่ได้อยู่บนร่างกาย แต่เป็นสิ่งที่ร่างกายสวมอยู่

หนังสือล้านนาเล่าจากฝั่งของตัวเองว่าชายชาวล้านนาสักจน **ดูเหมือนนุ่งกางเกงสีดำ** และชายที่ไม่มีรอยสักก็ให้ไปนุ่งซิ่นเสีย

บันทึกสเปนเรื่องชาววิซายันว่า ชายเปลือยที่มีรอยสัก "ดูเหมือน **สวมเกราะงดงาม** ที่สลักลายละเอียด"

ชาวคอร์ดิลเยราถือว่าการไม่มีรอยสักเท่ากับเปลือย ชาวซามัวเรียกชายที่ไม่ได้สักว่า **telefua** หรือ **telenoa** คือเปลือย ด้วยคำธรรมดา ไม่ใช่คำเปรียบ

when.label: Cook's first voyage, and Mai in London

text.what: English had no single word for the practice until Cook's crew brought one back from Polynesia.
text.story:
*Tatau* went into English as *tattoo* and swallowed everything else. Every tradition on this site is now described in English with a Samoan word, including the ones that had their own perfectly good nouns: *irezumi*, *godna*, *deq*, *kakiniq*, *sak*.

*Inference —* that is not only a linguistic accident. It is why the English-language record treats Pacific tattooing as the default case and everything else as a variation on it, and it is visible in the coverage count on this site: the traditions with the most language editions written about them are mostly the ones the eighteenth-century voyages reached first.

names.said: Counted in Wikipedia language editions, per tradition

text.what: Every tradition on this site that has a Wikipedia article, ranked by how many languages wrote one.
text.story:
The measurement is crude and that is the point: it is a count of attention, not of importance. Each tradition here names its article, and the harvest asks the Wikimedia API how many language editions carry it.

*Inference —* the shape of the answer is predictable before you run it, which is itself the finding. The traditions with the most editions are the ones eighteenth- and nineteenth-century European voyages met first and wrote up in European languages; the ones with the fewest are inland, upland, and were written about, if at all, in an administrative report.

The Lanna leg tattoo does not appear at all. Not thinly — it has no article in any language, in a project with more than three hundred language editions, for a custom that covered the legs of every man in a kingdom.
text.notes: Counted at build time. A tradition with no named article is listed as having none rather than scored as zero.

when.label: From the first tattooed men brought to London to the last sideshows

text.what: For two and a half centuries, the main way a European saw a tattooed body was on a stage, with an entrance fee.
text.story:
Tattooed people from the Pacific and Southeast Asia were brought to Europe and displayed; later, European and American performers had themselves covered in order to be displayed. The human zoos and the sideshow ran on the same premise and often the same circuit.

*Inference —* a photograph of a tattooed person from this period is therefore rarely neutral evidence. It was made to be sold, the pose was chosen for the sale, and the caption was written by whoever was taking the money. This site uses those pictures where they are the only pictures, and says so beside them.

names.name: The leg-tattoo zone
names.said: Burma, the Shan States and Lanna — and the border is not the border

text.what: One custom, four peoples, and a boundary that runs through the middle of modern Thailand rather than along its edge.
text.story:
Put the sources side by side.

**Burma, 1882.** Shway Yoe: every up-country man is tattooed from the navel to below the kneecap. Not a single *taw-tha*, the sturdy man of the small towns and villages, is without it.

**The Shan States, 1910.** Milne: a Shan boy is a child until he is tattooed; the rule is both legs, waist to knee, and often on to the ankles. Shway Yoe adds that the Shans go further than the Burmese — up the back, to the nape, and among a chief's retainers, everywhere but palms and soles.

**Lanna.** The Lanna volume: men tattooed until it looked as if they wore black trousers, waist to ankle, torso, arms, fingers — and "this fashion was widespread among the Burmese and the Tai Yai, who tattoo yantras no less than the Lanna."

**Siam.** Milne, in the same paragraph where she says the Shans learned it from the Burmese: "the Siamese, who are so closely related to them, **tattoo themselves very slightly, or not at all**."

*Inference —* that last line is usually read as a fact about Thailand. It is a fact about **central** Thailand. Milne was comparing the Shan to Bangkok, and Lanna — which was a tributary kingdom, not a province, until 1899 — is on the other side of her comparison. The leg tattoo's territory is the Tai-Buddhist upland: Burma, the Shan States, the Tai Khuen and Tai Lue towns, and Lanna. **The edge of the zone runs through modern Thailand, roughly where Lanna ended, and the colonial record could not see it because it was reading the map by kingdoms.**

This is what the map on this page is drawing, and it is the one map on the site that no source draws for it.
text.notes: The zone is drawn from four written sources and one manuscript. It is not a survey, nobody counted tattooed men anywhere, and the outline is this project's reading rather than anyone's measurement.

when.label: Banned at the opening of Meiji; legalised under the occupation

text.what: Japan banned tattooing while presenting itself to the world, and foreigners immediately travelled there to be tattooed.
text.story:
The ban was about image. The practice continued underground, tattooists worked on visiting sailors and princes, and the association with criminality that the ban created outlasted the ban by three generations. Osaka's mayor was still surveying city employees about their tattoos in 2012, and the courts found against him.

The Ryukyus got their own prohibition in 1899, aimed at *hajichi* on women's hands. Taiwan's Atayal were banned from facial tattooing in 1930 by the same administration.

*Inference —* three bans, one state, sixty years, and each one targets the marks of a people being absorbed. The Meiji ban is usually told as a story about respectability. Seen with the other two, it is a story about who gets to look like themselves.

when.label: Conversion, and the loss of the tradition across the lowlands

text.what: Spain called the Visayans *Pintados*, the painted ones, described their tattoos in detail, and converted them out of the practice within two centuries.
text.story:
The Spanish accounts are careful and admiring. They describe the tattoo as clothing; they record that no tattooing was begun until a brave deed had been performed and that each further panel needed another; they note that men tattooed even their chins and around the eyes so that they appeared masked.

Then the same administration's church ended it. In the lowlands the tradition is gone and the description survives. In the Cordillera, where Spain never held the mountains, the practice survives and the Spanish description does not apply.

*Inference —* on this site that is the clearest natural experiment there is: one people, two zones, the same century, and the difference is entirely whether the coloniser could get there.

names.name: Stopped, and started again
names.said: The gap, measured in years, where both ends have a date

text.what: Several traditions here stopped and came back. Where both ends are datable, this site subtracts them and prints the gap.
text.story:
Fiji: one tattooist left by 1908; an artists' collective takes it up again in the 2010s. Inuit: missionaries and the schools; a revitalisation project from 2016. Māori: the 1907 Act; the resurgence from 1990. Okinawa: the 1899 prohibition; hands being marked again now.

The gaps run to roughly a century each. *Inference —* what carries a practice across a hundred years is not a book. In every case on this list the bridge is a person: the elders Hovak Johnston learned the stitch from, the seventy women Michael King interviewed in the 1970s, the museum objects the Veiqia Project worked from, and the grandmothers.

A practice with no living bearer left is a different problem, and the Lanna leg tattoo is in that category.
text.notes: Gaps are computed from the `break` field on each tradition and shown with both endpoints, so a reader can disagree with either.

names.name: Five thousand years
names.said: From the oldest marked skin to the newest studio

text.what: The dated points: bodies with marks on them, bans with statutes behind them, revivals with a year.
text.story:
The timeline holds three kinds of date and keeps them apart. **Bodies**: Ötzi, the Gebelein mummies, the Chinchorro man, the Ukok woman, the Cordilleran mummies, the Qilakitsoq women — each with the range its laboratory gave. **Instruments**: the Arku Cave tools. **Paper**: bans, acts, patents and the revivals.

*Inference —* the visible gap between the ancient bodies and the nineteenth-century paper is not a gap in the practice. It is a gap in what survives: skin needs ice, salt, sand or bog, and paper needs an administration. Between them, four thousand years of ordinary tattooing left neither.

text.what: The word each tradition uses for the tattoo, and what it meant before it meant that.
text.story:
Four families, and they line up with the method rather than with the geography.

**Prick** — Thai and Khmer *sak*, Inuktitut *kaki-*, Hindi *godna*, Kurdish *deq*, Croatian *sicanje*, Burmese *htoe*, Okinawan *hajichi*. Every one of them is a poking tradition, and the word is the verb for what the needle does.

**Strike** — Samoan and Polynesian *tatau*, Māori *tā*, Marquesan *patu*. Every one of them is a tapping tradition, and the word is the verb for the mallet.

**Pattern** — Austronesian *batok*, *patik*, *burik*; Northern Thai *lai*. The word is the design, and it is the same word used for the pattern on a pot or a cloth.

**Write** — Atayal *ptasan*; and in Lanna, the tool for tattooing is the same *lek char* stylus used to write a palm-leaf manuscript.

*Inference —* a language names the tattoo after whichever part of it that culture finds most salient: the movement, the tool, the design, or the literacy. Four answers, and none of them is "the picture".

text_th.what: คำที่แต่ละธรรมเนียมใช้เรียกรอยสัก และความหมายของคำนั้นก่อนจะแปลว่ารอยสัก
text_th.story:
สี่ตระกูล และเรียงตามวิธี ไม่ใช่ตามภูมิศาสตร์

**แทง** — ไทยและเขมร *สัก* อินุกติตุต *kaki-* ฮินดี *godna* เคิร์ด *deq* โครเอเชีย *sicanje* พม่า *ထိုး* ทั้งหมดเป็นธรรมเนียมแบบแทง

**ตอก** — ซามัว *tatau* เมารี *tā* มาร์เคซัส *patu* ทั้งหมดเป็นธรรมเนียมแบบตอก

**ลาย** — ออสโตรนีเซียน *batok* และคำว่า *ลาย* ในภาษาเหนือ

**เขียน** — อาตายัล *ptasan* และทางล้านนา เครื่องมือสักคือเหล็กจารเล่มเดียวกับที่ใช้เขียนใบลาน
